When we launched Patchwork CI, we promised it would always be free for open source. Some people told us we were crazy and asked how we would make money.

Today we run on 1,200 repositories, and about 900 of them are open source.

One thing we learned along the way surprised me. Across all those repos, 1 in 7 CI failures turned out to be a flaky test. That is a lot of developer time spent on red builds that were never real failures.

Open source gave us more than users. It gave us data, feedback, and a community. Our most-requested feature, GitLab support, came straight from OSS maintainers, and we shipped it on November 12.

Giving back is not charity. It is strategy.

#OpenSource #DevOps #CI #DeveloperExperience #BuildInPublic

Losing our first big customer was the best thing that ever happened to Ledgerline.

So we listened, we learned, and we built.

Today, we serve 38 customers, and 11 of them rely on custom fields.

The lesson is that your biggest setback can become your biggest breakthrough. Lean into the hard feedback. Your customers are telling you what to build, and you just have to listen.

What's a loss that shaped your company?

We built an app we were proud of, and almost nobody used it.

When we launched Rotaship, we put a lot of work into a sleek, modern mobile app. We assumed restaurant staff would like it.

In the first month, only 12% of staff opened it.

That was when we understood the real problem. We were not solving anything for these teams. We were adding another task to their day.

Restaurant teams do not want another app. They already work through WhatsApp.

So in 2025 we made a difficult decision and moved everything into WhatsApp.

The results were clear. We now reach 140 outlets, and the median reply time to shift messages is under 20 minutes.

The lesson for us was to meet users where they already are, rather than asking them to change how they work. Sometimes that means letting go of the thing you were most attached to.

Our first production run at Shelfwise did not go as planned. 400 labels shipped with a faulty battery contact.

As a young hardware startup, it would have been easy to cut corners. That is not who we are. We decided to recall and replace every one of those 400 labels at our own cost. It set us back about $7,000. Painful? Absolutely. Worth it? 100%. Trust is everything.

We did not stop there. We introduced a 100% contact test at the factory, and since then we have had zero contact failures across 6,000 labels.

Mistakes do not define you. How you respond to them does. To all the hardware founders out there: own your mistakes, fix them fast, and build systems so they never happen again.
